newsitem.title: CANADA: EU, US trade chiefs discuss aircraft subsidies.
newsitem.headline: EU, US trade chiefs discuss aircraft subsidies.

text.p: European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan told U.S. Trade Representative Charlene Barshefsky on Friday that Europe was concerned about the effectiveness of an agreement limiting government subsidies to aircraft industries.
"We discussed the importance of taking seriously our concerns about the operations of the aircraft agreement," Brittan told reporters after meeting Barshefsky for more than an hour.
The two trade chiefs were in Toronto attending a meeting of the so-called "Quad" trading partners -- the United States, European Union, Canada and Japan.

Brittan said Europe was concerned that "a lot of American subsidies are slipping through" the 1992 Trans-Atlantic agreement that limits direct and indirect government subsidies to aircraft industries.
"We do not accept that proposition at all; at the same time the U.S. has some concerns about European practices," Barshefsky told reporters.
She said U.S. and EU officials would continue discussing the issue in June, but the United States would not agree to any emergency consultations.

The European Union raised concerns about the agreement after Boeing Co and McDonnell Douglas Corp announced merger plans. European Competition Commissioner Karl Van Miert is undertaking an investigation of the merger, which would create the largest aerospace company in the world.
Brittan said he also raised concerns about a series of mutual recognition agreements in which authorities would recognize each other's standards and testing procedures on a number of products.
The two sides have completed work on five agreements covering telecommunications equipment, electrical products, electromagnetic capabilities, pleasure boats and veterinary medicine.
Two agreements covering pharmaceuticals and medical devices have yet to be completed.
Both sides want them done in time for the EU-U.S. summit at the end of the month, but Brittan said the outstanding issues involving regulation of pharmaceuticals and medical devices must be settled.
"Unless there is real change on the American side, it is not going to happen," Brittan told reporters.

Brittan said he also raised concerns about a Massachusetts law barring government agencies from engaging in commercial transactions with companies that do business with Burma. A U.S. official said Washington was working with state authorities to address Europe's concerns.
